hlni.insight: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive.
hlni.audienceGap: Students assume a degree is defined by broad labels rather than specific output requirements.
hlni.viewerChange: Learns to look for assessment criteria instead of degree names.
hlni.support: The method separates three different pieces of information; it does not assume particular course content.
hlni.payoff: Student shifts focus from degree titles to specific task-assessment pairs.

creativeAngle: Moving from degree labels to assessment criteria
objective: Help students compare B.Com and BBA by focusing on output requirements rather than labels
targetAudience: +2 students seeking academic depth and well-supported course and career decisions

shots.name: The Degree Dilemma
shots.visual: A student looking at two brochures labeled B.Com and BBA with a confused expression.
shots.dialogue: Choosing between B.Com and BBA feels like guessing.
shots.cameraPerformance: Close up on the student's face.

shots.name: The Label Trap
shots.visual: Student circles the degree names on a paper, looking frustrated.
shots.dialogue: These names don't show what I actually have to produce.

shots.name: The Audit Shift
shots.visual: Student puts brochures aside and draws a grid, referencing them to define the audit context.
shots.cameraPerformance: Over the shoulder shot onto the paper.

shots.name: Filling the Grid
shots.visual: Student writes in the grid using the retail shop case study example.
shots.dialogue: Map your task, grading criteria, and feedback.
shots.onscreenText: Example: Task: Write proposal. Graded on: ? Feedback: ?

shots.name: The Concrete Question
shots.visual: Student points to the question marks in the grid while looking at the camera.
shots.dialogue: What specific criteria determine if this proposal is successful?
shots.onscreenText: What specific criteria determine if this proposal is successful?

shots.name: Final Action
shots.visual: Student picks up the audit sheet to prepare for a course inquiry.
shots.dialogue: Take this specific question to your next inquiry.
shots.cameraPerformance: Wide shot of student at desk.

productionNotes.camera: Stable shots with clear focus on the worksheet
productionNotes.editing: Rhythmic cuts matching the audit steps
productionNotes.sound: Ambient room tone, pen scratching on paper

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Students should audit assessment criteria rather than degree titles to make informed choices.

selected.title: The Assessment Audit
selected.audienceGap: Students assume a degree is defined by broad labels rather than specific output requirements.
selected.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
selected.viewerChange: Learns to look for assessment criteria instead of degree names.
selected.concept: A student breaks down a sample case study into three columns: product, criteria, feedback.
selected.support: The method separates three different pieces of information; it does not assume particular course content.
methodSteps: Ask what criterion is used to assess it.
Ask what feedback is available; mark unknown answers as questions.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
selected.visibleProof: A three-column question sheet turns one vague preference into a concrete unanswered question.
selected.payoff: Student shifts focus from degree titles to specific task-assessment pairs.
selected.limitations: This is a question-forming aid, not a degree ranking, aptitude test or prediction of success.

demonstration.input: A sample business case study about a retail shop's inventory.
demonstration.visibleInput: Example: Task: Write proposal. Graded on: ? Feedback: ?
demonstration.observation: The student identifies that knowing the task isn't enough to know the goal.
demonstration.nextQuestion: What specific criteria determine if this proposal is successful?

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
One unlabeled example does not prove which category or programme contains it. An exclusive claim needs information that actually links the example to that category.

conceptSelection.contrast: Pre-story comparison selected different grounded insights and mechanisms: Trust = assessment_questions / three_column_audit; Connection = task_question_journal / peer_observation_journal; Discovery = insufficient_information / missing_evidence_reveal. Each has an illustrative input, observable result and next question. This is not editorial approval.
